A novel multi-agent system based event location and isolation approach is proposed for a modern power distribution system using synchronized current and voltage from a limited number of PMUs. The developed multi-agent framework uses a decentralized hierarchical agent scheme and consists of heterogeneous agent types, with the PMUs defined as the main computational agents. The agents receive their local synchrophasor measurements and perform the algorithm by communicating with their neighboring agents to locate the faulted bus with minimal communication messages. The new fault location algorithm is a two-step process: first, the agents identify the faulted section using impedance comparison and isolate the faulted zone; second, the corresponding agents within the zone identify the faulted bus using voltage comparison and send the bus information to the control center. Studies are conducted by interconnecting the IEEE 34-bus network with distributed energy resources developed in PSCAD/EMTDC and a multi-agent system implemented on the JADE platform. Simulations of various test cases verify the efficacy of the proposed multi-agent scheme in accurately locating various faults occurring in the distribution network.

title: Prior Knowledge-Guided Active Learning Network for Multi-Source Partial Discharge Diagnosis in Gas-Insulated Switchgear
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence presents both opportunities and significant challenges for multi-source partial discharge (PD) diagnosis in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS), but challenges remain due to insufficient incorporation of underlying physical mechanisms, limited labeled data, noise interference, class imbalance, and difficulties in decoupling mixed PD sources. To address these issues, this paper proposes a prior knowledge–guided active learning network (PKGALN) for multi-source PD diagnosis in GIS, in which physics-related PD characteristics are explicitly embedded into the model design under a limited-label regime. Specifically, a prior knowledge–guided U-former is constructed by incorporating physically interpretable PD descriptors (e.g., time–frequency statistical features reflecting discharge behavior) as global guidance for feature learning, while a scale-guided convolutional–wavelet encoder enhances denoising and multi-scale representation capability. In addition, a multi-label decoupling recognition module is designed to explicitly handle mixed PD sources, and a distribution-balanced loss is adopted to alleviate severe class imbalance. To further reduce annotation cost, an adaptive active learning strategy is introduced, dynamically balancing uncertainty and diversity during sample selection. Experimental results on both laboratory and field datasets demonstrate that PKGALN achieves diagnostic accuracies of 96.39% and 93.26%, respectively, using only 10% of labeled samples. By leveraging limited labeled data, the proposed approach enables robust diagnosis of both single-source and multi-source PDs.

title: Analysis of Electric Field Shielding Characteristics on Residential Platforms and Optimization of Shielding Position Near 1000 kV Double-Circuit Transmission Lines on the Same Tower
abstract: The electric field strength beneath 1000 kV ultra-high-voltage transmission lines is relatively high, posing a risk of excessive electric field exposure in the presence of nearby buildings. Shielding wires are an effective technical measure to mitigate excessive electric field strength at sensitive locations; however, optimal performance depends on the appropriate selection of shielding parameters such as wire size and placement. In this study, a 6 m × 6 m building platform was constructed beneath a 1000 kV double-circuit transmission line mounted on a single tower. Shielding wires with heights of 5 m, 6 m, and 7 m were installed. The electric field distribution above the building, as well as the shielding effects, were analyzed. The optimal positioning of the shielding wires was also investigated. The results indicate that the electric field on the upper surface of the platform closest to the transmission line side can reach 5 kV/m, while the electric field on the second-level platform can reach up to 7.5 kV/m. A single shielding wire can reduce the electric field strength by 21.7%, whereas multiple wires can achieve reductions of more than 30% . We convert the above electric field model into a mathematical model and propose an optimization method for the shielding wires position. When the height of the shielding wire is less than 8 m, the optimal placement is approximately directly above the sensitive point. These findings provide practical guidance for mitigating electric fields near sensitive areas and offer a technical foundation for the design and installation of shielding wires.

title: Transmission Line Galloping Detection System Based on an Improved PIDNet
abstract: The galloping phenomenon of transmission lines, exacerbated by extreme weather, poses a significant threat to grid stability and power supply. The practical application of conventional sensor-based methods is limited by high deployment costs and low adaptability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an end-to-end galloping detection system based on video monitoring. An improved PIDNet forms the segmentation backbone, incorporating a Line-features Interactive Two-Branch (LITB) network to leverage line orientation priors, a Detail Recovery Decoder (DRD) to enhance line continuity, and an Edge Perception Module (EPM) to refine boundary segmentation against complex backgrounds. Optical flow analysis is subsequently employed to quantify transmission line displacement and determine galloping states. Experimental results demonstrate performance improvements of 6.9% in mIoU, 4.23% in mAcc, and 4.8% mDice over popular segmentation models. The proposed embedded detection system achieves an accuracy of 84.00%, a recall of 90.31%, and an F1-score of 87.17% when deployed on edge devices.

title: Fully Actuated Control of Point-to-Point VSC–HVDC Links for Frequency and DC Voltage Regulation in Asynchronous AC Systems
abstract: Grid-forming (GFM) VSC–HVDC systems can provide frequency support to ac grids, particularly in point-to-point VSC–HVDC links interconnecting asynchronous ac systems. However, large power variations commanded for frequency support may jeopardize the dc-link voltage stability. To simultaneously enhance frequency support and preserve dc-link voltage regulation, this paper develops two robust controllers for the rectifier and inverter stations based on the fully actuated control (FAC) theory. FAC provides a systematic diffeomorphism-based transformation that converts the original under-actuated and strongly coupled station dynamics into an equivalent fully actuated form, thereby revealing virtual input channels and enabling direct shaping of the key dc-voltage- and frequency-related states for controller synthesis. In the transformed coordinates, multiple perturbations—including stochastic load variations, parameter uncertainties, and external disturbances—are aggregated as lumped disturbances. High-gain disturbance observers are then designed for both stations to estimate the lumped disturbances. Leveraging the observer-based estimates, a robust sliding-mode control law is formulated in the fully actuated coordinates to compensate the aggregated uncertainties, thereby ensuring resilient frequency support while maintaining dc-link voltage regulation. Simulation studies on two test systems validate the effectiveness of the proposed controllers in regulating the dc-link voltage and supporting grid frequency under multiple scenarios.

title: Thermomechanical Modeling of Clamping Forces in Power Transformers With Field Data Validation
abstract: Maintaining the mechanical integrity of a power transformer during large fault currents requires a clamping system that exerts sufficient compressive forces on the windings. This paper presents a thermomechanical model for the clamping force in a power transformer. The model predicts changes in clamping forces due to operating conditions, such as load and ambient temperatures, to indicate when the transformer is most vulnerable to mechanical failures. The model was tested and evaluated on one year of operational data collected from a 40 MVA ONAN transformer equipped with extensive temperature monitoring and novel clamping force sensors. By using only transformer design data, fundamental material parameters and results from the heat run test, the model was able to replicate the general trends observed in the measured clamping force. The model was able to predict the daily mean clamping force throughout the year with a mean absolute error of 6.6 kN, which corresponds to 2.9% of the initial clamping force at the start of the year. For daily variations, i.e., the difference between maximum and minimum clamping force for each day, the model was able to predict variations with a mean error of 2.1 kN. However, the model overestimates the changes in clamping force, as it is too sensitive to changes in loading and ambient temperature.

title: Sinusoidality Index
abstract: Maintaining sinusoidal or near-sinusoidal operating conditions in electrical systems is essential, as is their accurate assessment. This letter proposes a novel metric, namely the sinusoidality index, which quantifies the instantaneous deviation of the trajectory of an ac voltage vector with respect to a circle under any periodic operating conditions. This metric differs from conventional Fourier-based estimations by accounting for the trajectory of the waveform rather than its spectral decomposition. A variety of examples illustrates the properties of the proposed metric and highlights insights that may not be captured by conventional approaches.

title: Investigation of the External Thermal Resistance of Cables in Backfills and Duct Banks
abstract: The Neher/McGrath paper and IEC Standard 60287-2-1 provide formulas for calculating the external thermal resistance of cables installed in backfills or duct banks. In this context, the backfill or duct bank is represented as a circular isothermal surface, assuming that the thermal resistances of both are equivalent. The 2023 edition of IEC Standard 60287-2-1 introduces a table of geometric factors to calculate the radius of the equivalent circle. In contrast, earlier editions relied on an analytical formula that assumed the backfill's width-to-height ratio was between 1/3 and 3. This paper investigates modeling problems arising from the application of the new IEC standard 60287-2-1 to cables installed in duct banks and backfills. The findings indicate that assumptions in the IEC standard for modeling the external thermal resistance of cables may lead to significant errors. As a result, the paper proposes a new approach that addresses weaknesses in the standard approach. The new approach is verified through a finite-element analysis. Several numerical examples illustrate the differences between the proposed approach and the results based on the standard analysis.

title: A Constrained Formulation for Simultaneous Line Parameter Estimation and Instrument Transformer Calibration
abstract: The process of calibrating instrument transformers (ITs) has been greatly simplified by using phasor measurement unit (PMU) data since this process eliminates the need for (a) additional hardware, and (b) taking ITs offline. However, such simplification comes at the cost of knowing the line parameters, whose estimation using PMU data in turn requires calibrated ITs. To solve this interdependency problem, we propose a novel framework that incorporates power system domain knowledge as constraints to perform simultaneous line parameter estimation and IT calibration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with simulated and real PMU data as well as for a power system application that uses both PMU data and line parameter information.

title: High-Sensitivity Zero-Sequence Pilot Protection for High-Impedance Faults in Low-Resistance Grounded Distribution Networks
abstract: Reliable detection and rapid isolation of single-phase-to-ground faults (SPGFs) in low-resistance grounded systems (LRGSs) are critical for power utilization safety. However, the conventional zero-sequence (ZS) overcurrent protection method exhibits significant limitations in speed and sensitivity under arcing or high-impedance faults (HIFs). This paper presents a dual-criteria-based pilot protection scheme for HIFs in LRGSs using ZS distribution characteristics. The characteristics of the ZS admittance ratio at the fault point for SPGFs are analyzed, whose minimum value is significantly greater than that at unfaulted points under any situation. The ZS admittance ratio at both ends of the fault section further amplifies the above fault features based on the ZS voltages/currents distribution, which serves as the primary criterion for protection design when protective relays at both terminals are activated. The auxiliary protection logic, a supplementary criterion under HIFs or terminal faults, is triggered by a rise in the single-ended ZS impedance during internal faults. The MATLAB/Simulink simulation and the real-time digital simulator (RTDS) hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a fault resistance tolerance of 4 kΩ within one power-frequency cycle. Moreover, it maintains reliable performance under challenging conditions, including arcing faults and the integration of distributed generators.

title: Downscaling Method for Ground Flash Density in Transmission Line Corridors Considering Terrain Effects
abstract: Ground Flash Density (GFD) serves as a critical parameter for evaluating the lightning strike risk of transmission lines. It is typically derived from the statistical analysis of data monitored by Lightning Location Systems. However, constrained by the limited sample size of ground flashes and the detection accuracy of Lightning Location Systems, the spatial resolution of GFD is relatively low. To enhance the spatial resolution of GFD along transmission line corridors, this paper proposes a downscaling method of GFD based on the Monte Carlo method considering micro-terrain conditions. For a given original grid area, considering the influence of terrain on lightning, the lightning strike point is determined by the lightning leader fractal model, thereby generating a simulated dataset of ground flash samples dataset. The original grid is further divided into multiple subunits, and the GFD of subunit is calculated by combining the grid average ground flash density statistics, ultimately yielding the high spatial resolution ground flash density. The proposed method is used to calculate GFD in the actual grid area and the effectiveness of the method is verified.

title: Joint Type Diagnosis and Severity Assessment of Partial Discharge in Gas-Insulated Switchgear via Multi-Task Learning
abstract: Partial discharge (PD) is a key indicator of insulation health in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS). It is widely used for condition monitoring in high-voltage power systems. However, the diverse intensities and underlying fault mechanisms of PD often result in complex and variable signal patterns. Traditional single-task learning approaches struggle to capture this complexity and generalize across multiple diagnostic objectives. To address these challenges, we propose PD-MTNet, a multi-task learning framework for simultaneous PD type diagnosis and severity assessment. The framework adopts an attention-enhanced lightweight backbone to extract robust shared representations, tailored to the multi-scale and sparse nature of PRPD data. By highlighting salient discharge regions and suppressing background responses, the backbone effectively captures physically meaningful features across phase–amplitude scales. A multi-path hybrid module is then employed to decouple task-specific features according to their diagnostic mechanisms, facilitating more discriminative representations for each task. This design, together with the shared feature learning strategy, enhances intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. This design improves robustness to ambiguous boundaries and noisy labels, resulting in more stable and physically consistent diagnostic performance. Experimental results demonstrate that PD-MTNet achieves classification accuracies of 97.92% for PD type diagnosis and 95.19% for severity assessment, validating its effectiveness and generalization capability in complex PD diagnostic scenarios.

title: A Novel Transient Disturbance Waveform Compression Method in Distribution Networks Based on Dictionary Learning
abstract: The distribution network with a large-scale integration of distributed renewable energy sources exhibits more complex dynamic behavior. The widespread deployment of high-resolution waveform monitoring in distribution networks is hindered by the massive data transmission and storage requirements. To mitigate this communication bottleneck, this paper proposes a novel transient disturbance waveform compression method in distribution networks based on dictionary learning. A new framework for disturbance waveform compression on terminal side and reconstruction on master station side has been proposed to outline the offline learning and online decomposition steps. Then a determination method of the start and end times of transient disturbance waveforms based on the relative energy acceleration operator (REAO) has been proposed for disturbance waveform segmentation, which clarifies the disturbance processes that need to be monitored. To improve the decomposition and reconstruction efficiency, an overcomplete dictionary design method that considers feature redundancy within the dictionary based on clustering pruning optimized K-SVD (CPK-SVD) has been proposed. The redundant atoms in the dictionary are pruned based on Gaussian mixture model (GMM) clustering method after feature extraction. Simulation and field recorded waveform data tests show that the proposed method can achieve a compression ratio of over 10 while ensuring measurement accuracy.

title: IGBT Open-Circuit Fault Detection and Localization Method for Cascaded H-Bridge Stage of Power Electronic Transformer
abstract: The rectifier stage of power electronic transformers (PETs) commonly employs either a cascaded H-bridge (CHB) or a modular multilevel converter (MMC) topology. Due to its high modularity, scalability, and ease of redundancy design, the CHB topology is widely adopted in PETs. However, the use of numerous power electronic devices in PETs increases the probability of faults. In this paper, a novel fault detection and localization method is proposed for the rapid identification of IGBT open-circuit faults in the CHB stages of PETs. A mathematical model of the CHB grid-side voltage is established, which contains abundant harmonic information. The harmonic characteristics of the grid-side voltage under different IGBT open-circuit faults are analyzed, revealing that the amplitude and phase of even-order carrier frequency harmonics depend on the location of the faulty H-bridges. Based on this characteristic, the fault region is identified. By adjusting the modulation scheme of specific H-bridges and analyzing the resulting variations in the grid-side voltage, multiple IGBT open-circuit faults can be accurately localized. The proposed method utilizes the characteristic harmonics of the H-bridge port theoretical voltage as a reference, thereby reducing fault-identification time and remaining unaffected by load conditions. Its effectiveness is validated through PSCAD/EMTDC simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments.

title: Temperature-Based Hybrid Modeling for Heating Power Prediction and Fault Detection in Power Transformers
abstract: Accurate estimation of internal heating power is essential for transformer thermal assessment and fault diagnosis. However, the multi-physics coupling and nonlinear heat transfer in oil-immersed transformers make it difficult to infer heating power directly from external temperatures using purely physical models. This paper proposes a hybrid temperature-based framework that integrates physical understanding with data-driven learning. The physical thermal–electrical model is used to reveal the nonlinear temperature–power relationships, guiding feature selection via mutual information (MI) analysis. Selected temperature features are then applied to a random forest (RF) regressor for heating power prediction. Experiments on a thermally equivalent scaled prototype of a 500 kV power transformer, involving 28 operating cases under both normal and fault conditions, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high prediction accuracy, with an average test $R^{2}$ of 0.9956 and a test mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 2.27%. Moreover, deviations in predicted heating power under constant load effectively indicate localized thermal anomalies. The results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach offers a practical and interpretable solution for transformer condition monitoring using only external temperature measurements.

title: A Segmented Insulation Assessment Method of Power Cable Based on EWV Inversion
abstract: Compared with the traditional holistic insulation assessment (HIA) methods, which can only provide the insulation condition information of whole cables, segmented insulation assessment (SIA) can provide the insulation condition information of each cable segment, thereby enhancing cable maintenance efficiency. In the past, SIA was achieved by estimating the attenuation coefficient through quantitatively calculating reflected wave amplitudes. However, multiple signal reflections within the cable cause cross-coupling among reflected wave amplitudes, leading to poor generalizability and inaccuracy in SIA. In this article, an SIA method based on velocity inversion using compressive subspace multiple signal classification (CS-MUSIC) is proposed to avoid the problem of the past method. The idea of the proposed method is that electromagnetic wave velocity (EWV) in a power cable is associated with the insulation condition of the cable. The more serious the cable insulation aging, the slower the EWV. Besides, a power cable can naturally be divided into several segments by power cable joints. Consequently, if the EWV in each cable segment can be assessed, the EWV can be used to evaluate the insulation condition of each cable segment. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed method is verified through simulation, experiment, and a 10kV power cable field test.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Terminal DC System for Large-Scale Renewable Integration: Topology and Coordinated Control
abstract: As DC power projects transition toward phased construction and higher voltage levels, interconnecting existing systems to form a multi-voltage-level DC grid is a pragmatic choice that balances the wide-area integration of large-scale renewable energy with the maximization of legacy asset utilization. While DC/DC transformer (DCT) topologies provide viable technical paths, scaling them to ultra-high-voltage applications involves considerations such as full-scale hardware requirements and isolation transformer design. To facilitate more flexible phased expansion, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Multi-Terminal DC (HMTDC) system with Coordinated Primary and Secondary Control (CPSC). The topology employs Multi-Voltage-Level Interconnecting MMCs (MVLI-MMCs) rated for the inter-system voltage differential rather than full terminal voltage, enabling gigawatt-level power exchange through significantly reduced converter capacity. The CPSC combines distributed droop-based primary control for rapid disturbance rejection with secondary optimization that coordinates power margins and voltage quality across subsystems. Comprehensive time-domain simulations demonstrate that the proposed framework not only optimizes cross-level power flows but also ensures fault ride-through and rapid recovery under severe AC/DC contingencies, thereby providing a techno-economically viable pathway for evolving multi-voltage-level DC grids.

title: Generalized Circuit Modeling Method of the Low-Frequency Dynamics for Multi-Terminal AC/DC Hybrid System
abstract: A generalized circuit modeling method is proposed to investigate the low-frequency oscillation problem of the AC/DC hybrid system. Firstly, Based on analogy method, the conversion from control block diagram model to circuit model is realized, and the single-port circuit model of photovoltaic-voltage source converter (PV-VSC) is established. Furthermore, in order to give consideration to the dynamic response of the DC side, the two-port circuit model of voltage source converter (VSC) is built by making use of the unified energy path theory and the concept of energy hub. Next, on the basis of the system topology, the circuit model of AC/DC hybrid system can be acquired, which provides a reliable method for the problem of low-frequency oscillation in high-permeability new energy grid connection. More importantly, topology and circuit theory/method can be employed to investigate the dynamic response characteristics of AC/DC side interfaces under different types of disturbances, without constructing complex differential equations. Finally, the validity of the proposed modeling method is proved by building the MATLAB/Simulink model and physical experiment.

title: Equivalent Inertia Mechanism Modeling and Magnitude-Phase Characteristics Analysis of Grid-Supporting MMC-HVDC Systems
abstract: The grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems emulate synchronous generator characteristics to enable efficient power transmission while providing frequency support. However, existing studies lack analytical insights into the equivalent inertia and time-varying supporting mechanism under different control strategies. To address this, an equivalent inertia analytical model for grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems is firstly established from a frequency-domain perspective. The proposed models can accurately describe the equivalent inertia and the time-varying characteristics under different control modes, and their validity and correctness are verified through comparative simulation case studies. Based on the established model, the magnitude-phase supporting characteristics of grid-supporting MMC-HVDC are analyzed. The amplitude |HMMC(s)| is derived to evaluate the magnitude of inertia support capability provided by the MMC-HVDC, while the resonance frequency ωpeak is employed to analyze the phase-delay characteristics of the maximum inertia supporting power and the influence on frequency recovery. Besides, the supporting mechanism of different parameters on the equivalent inertia are analyzed, and the dominant characteristics of these parameters during different stages of frequency recovery is revealed. Simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed model and conclusions.

title: Discrimination of Tree-Contact High-Impedance and Flame Faults in Distribution Networks via Zero-Sequence Voltage Monitoring
abstract: Tree-contact high-impedance faults (THIF) and flame faults are common fault types in the forest area. Their mitigation and prevention are crucial to the management of distribution network faults. However, the signals of these faults are so weak that existing zero-sequence protection methods cannot ensure effectiveness and accuracy during the early fault stage. To address this issue, this paper investigates the electro-thermal coupling mechanism during the fault evolution process. Fault resistance models are established for different fault types. Experiments on 10 kV and 35 kV distribution systems verify that the proposed models can effectively capture the time-varying characteristics of the faults. Then electrical characteristics are investigated during discharges by applying Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to the zero-sequence voltage. Feature parameters are obtained including Total Harmonic Distortion (THD), Power Spectral Entropy (PSE), Skewness (SKE) and Kurtosis (KUR) of the sub-fundamental spectral components. Statistical analysis is employed to mitigate the influence of individual sample variability. From the experimental results, the frequency domain characteristics of both THIF and flame faults are independent of voltage levels. THD of flame fault is significantly higher than that of THIF due to the unstable discharge path in the flame. Conversely, THIF shows higher SKE and KUR because of low-frequency turbulence in the flame. The combined unstable discharge channel and turbulence cause PSE to be significantly higher in flame fault than in THIF. This research provides a methodological basis for fault classification and prevention for both 10 kV and 35 kV distribution lines.

title: A Unified Reliability Modeling Framework for MMC Considering Flexible Submodule Configuration and Preventive Maintenance
abstract: Conventional analytical models for engineering-scale modular multilevel converters (MMCs) face significant challenges in reliability assessment, particularly in incorporating preventive maintenance (PM) and redundancy. This paper proposes a simulation-based reliability modeling approach using the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method, which tracks the system-level operational state evolution while considering PM. The approach enables the determination of reliability indices for engineering-scale systems and identifies the optimal fixed PM intervals and redundancy submodule (SM) configurations. Furthermore, it enables flexible adjustment of both the number and type of SMs within a unified framework for reliability assessment. Based on extensive simulation and validation, the method demonstrates its effectiveness in supporting reliability analysis and system design, offering a general framework for practical applications.

title: Quantitative Metrics for Evaluating Grid Strength Across Power System Stability Domains: A Review
abstract: The increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is reducing grid strength, making accurate assessment essential for reliable and stable power system operation. Quantitative metrics offer systematic and practical tools for evaluating grid strength, supporting both planning and operational decisions. This paper provides a comprehensive review of quantitative metrics for grid strength assessment across static, small-signal, and transient stability domains. Metrics are categorized and discussed in terms of their definitions, derivation methods, advantages, and limitations, with particular attention to the effects of IBR interactions, network topology, and control strategies. Relevant stability criteria, practical applicability, and recommended threshold values are also summarized. This review aims to support system planners and operators in selecting and applying appropriate grid strength metrics in power systems with high IBR penetration.

title: Design and Verification of Novel Self-Voltage Sharing Vacuum Interrupter for Multi-Break VCBs in GIS
abstract: A key challenge for multi-break vacuum circuit breakers (VCBs) in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) is the design of compact voltage grading solutions for vacuum interrupters (VIs). This paper addresses the non-uniform voltage distribution across VI shields and series-connected breaks in VCBs that is caused by the significantly increased stray capacitances in GIS. To address these issues, we propose a novel self-voltage sharing capacitor pattern (SSCP), and the equivalent circuit of the VI with SSCP is analyzed. Simulations of the SSCP and the conventional grading capacitor pattern (CGCP) were conducted, and the maximum external electric field strength of the VI with SSCP was reduced by 53.6%, while the temperature rise was also decreased by 33.9%. A 40.5-kV VI prototype with SSCP was developed based on ring capacitors, external shields, and integrated encapsulation. Experimental results for series-connected VIs with SSCP demonstrate that the potential distributions among the shields and breaks approach the ideal values. The withstand voltage of series-connected VIs with SSCP is increased by 12.5%, and the temperature rise is decreased by 32.2%. The feasibility of the VI with SSCP has been verified, providing a compact voltage-sharing design reference for ultra-high-voltage multi-break VCBs in GIS.

title: Privacy-Preserving Coordination of Heterogeneous Electrolyzers: A Federated Reinforcement Learning Approach With Safety Guarantees
abstract: The complementarity between high-flexibility Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) and low-cost Alkaline (ALK) electrolyzers contributes to the synergistic development of green power and hydrogen sectors. However, wide-range renewable power fluctuations impose technical challenges on the optimal power allocation among these heterogeneous PEM and ALK units, which might result in safety violations and operational inefficiency. To address these challenges, this study proposes a privacy-preserving, physics-informed federated multi-agent control framework. Specifically, the architecture leverages a federated learning paradigm to aggregate decentralized strategies with limited direct data exchange, while incorporating an LSTM-enhanced algorithm to resolve partial observability by tracking long-timescale multiphysics dynamics like thermodynamic evolution and gas purity. Furthermore, a dual-tier proactive defense mechanism integrating a robust risk predictor with a quadratic programming projection layer is designed to strictly enforce hard physical constraints. Numerical results verify that the proposed approach effectively balances data privacy, physical safety, and precise regulation performance.

title: Dynamic Interaction Modeling and Stability Analysis for Grid-Connected Renewable Energy Systems With High Inertia Energy Storage Synchronous Condenser
abstract: The high inertia energy storage synchronous condenser (HIESSC), which integrates the doubly-fed machine technology with flywheel energy storage, has recently emerged as a promising means to support both frequency and voltage regulation in renewable energy sources (RESs). Despite its novelty, the impact of the HIESSC on system oscillations and the interactions among the control loops of RES stations remains unclear. This paper examines a grid-connected system comprising the HIESSC and a grid-connected converter with grid-following control (GCC-GFL). Firstly, a single-input-single-output interaction model is developed through equivalent block diagram transformations. By incorporating the grid-side coupling impedance and transfer functions of interacting subsystems, the proposed model reveals how the HIESSC modifies the dynamic characteristics of GCC-GFL through a feedback control perspective. Subsequently, the impact of HIESSC operating modes and operating points on the small-signal stability is analyzed. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed methods and analyses is validated by the experiments.

title: Carbon, Cost and Capacity: Weighted-Objective Charging of Electric Buses
abstract: The public transport sector is in the process of decarbonizing by electrifying its bus fleets. This results in challenges if the high electricity demand resulting from battery charging demand is confronted with limited grid capacity and high synchronicity at bus charging sites. In this paper, we explore weighted-objective scheduling for bus charging sites to minimize the emissions associated with charging processes and to aid the operation of the electricity grid by mitigating peak consumption. In particular, we discuss and validate optimization approaches for those individual objectives, as well as their weighted combination, based on data from a real-life bus charging site in the Netherlands. The simulation results show that compared to uncontrolled charging, power peaks can be reduced by up to 40%, while time-of-use emissions associated with the charging of electric buses are also reduced significantly. Furthermore, by using a baseload recorded at a German industrial site, we illustrate the flexibility potential offered by bus charging sites, and advocate that such sites should share a grid connection with other high-load assets.

title: Routing and Scheduling of Mobile Energy Storage Systems for Distribution Network Resilience Enhancement Based on a Hybrid Data-Model Driven Approach
abstract: Mobile Energy Storage Systems (MESSs) are critical for improving distribution network resilience under extreme weather events. However, the mathematical model for MESS routing and scheduling is essentially a high-dimensional mixed-integer nonlinear stochastic optimization problem. To accurately and rapidly obtain the routing and scheduling of MESSs and the optimal operation of distribution networks, a bi-level optimization of MESS routing and scheduling based on a hybrid data-model driven approach is proposed. In the upper level, the data-driven approach is achieved by the graph attention network multi-agent conservative soft actor-critic reinforcement learning (GMARL) to determine optimal routing decisions for MESS in the transportation network while taking into account traffic flow and road repair time uncertainties. The proposed GMARL takes full advantage of a graph attention network for feature extraction, and adopts the multi-agent conservative soft actor-critic to mitigate overestimation caused by out-of-distribution experiences, thereby effectively coordinating multiple MESSs to achieve the optimal strategy. In the lower level, a mixed-integer second-order cone programming is formulated to obtain optimal scheduling strategies for MESSs, reconfiguration and optimal power flow in the distribution network. Upon determining the scheduling strategies and amount of load recovery, the reward function value for each MESS can be calculated and used to update the neural network parameters of GMARL, thereby further optimizing the routing strategies of MESSs. Finally, case studies on an IEEE 33-bus active distribution network and a 12-node transportation network are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Available-Power-Constrained Coordinated Fault Voltage Support Control for Multiple Inverter-Interfaced DGs
abstract: The increasing prevalence of weak grid conditions necessitates that inverter-interfaced distributed generators (IIDGs) support voltage during faults to prevent further disturbances. However, maximizing IIDGs’ voltage support capability while respecting operational constraints to prevent unintended tripping remains challenging. This paper proposes an available-power-constrained coordinated fault voltage support control strategy for multiple IIDGs. First, based on the fault characteristics of resistive-inductive distribution networks (DN), a current reference strategy is developed to maximize each IIDG’s voltage support contribution. Then, considering constraints of non-fault-phase voltage and power fluctuation, the safe operating domain of each IIDG is derived. On this basis, an adaptive fault voltage support control framework is constructed, where a zonal clustering method enables communication free coordinated control among multiple IIDGs. In addition, the applicable condition of the proposed method is quantified using the grid short-circuit ratio (SCR) of the grid. Simulation results show that, for case of SCR lower than 3, the proposed method can improve the fault voltage of DNs by 30.8%.

title: A MADRL Driven Optimization Framework for Grid Node Inertia and Grid-Forming Converter Damping Characteristics in Microgrids
abstract: The integration of numerous new energy generators into the AC grid will diminish the inertia characteristics traditionally provided by synchronous generators, leading to frequency instability. The inertia and damping constants of the more widely used grid-forming converter (GFC) control methods are fixed. This paper proposes a multi-intelligent deep learning (MADRL) based optimization strategy to enhance the inertia and damping characteristics of GFCs. We begin by analyzing the constraints of the inertia that GFC source measurements can provide and propose a method for acquiring the inertia time constant (ITC) based on node active power and frequency. This method facilitates the partitioning of the distribution grid according to ITC values. Furthermore, we implement characteristic-enhanced branching to optimize inertia and damping characteristics through MADRL decision-making. Utilizing an IEEE-129 network with multiple new energy field stations, the experimental results demonstrate that this approach can increase the ITC of most nodes by over five times. In addition, we maintain frequency fluctuations within 0.01pu, representing a reduction of more than 95% compared to virtual synchronous generator control, while the maximum frequency transient fluctuation decreases by 81%. Furthermore, through comparative experiments and transfer learning, it can be demonstrated that this method possesses sufficient superiority and plug-and-play capability.

title: Shaping the Q-U Droop Characteristic of Grid-Forming Converters From the Perspective of Constant Voltage Control
abstract: With the increasing penetration rate of variable renewable energy (VRE) and other inverter-based resources (IBR) in power systems, system inertia and strength are being continuously weakened. Grid-forming (GFM) technology, adaptable to weak grids, has attracted widespread attention. The GFM Q-U droop control is widely adopted in practice, but it is challenging to tune key parameters, such as initial voltage reference value and droop coefficient, therefore, the adaptability and effectiveness of voltage support is difficult to ensure. To take the advantages of GFM converters as voltage sources, adopting constant voltage control (CVC) seems to be a better choice. This paper clarifies the implicit internal connection between CVC and droop control, indicating that the droop characteristic does not inherently depend on droop control, but should be regarded as a natural external port performance under internal CVC. Based on above analysis, a novel shaping method for Q-U droop characteristic of GFM converters from the perspective of CVC using virtual impedance is proposed. The virtual impedance in the proposed method is straightforward to set due to its explicit physical meaning, and the method performs well in strong adaptability and robustness for both islanded and grid-connected modes. Finally, the conclusions and the control effectiveness are verified by theoretical analysis, simulation, and experimental results.

title: Short-Term Frequency Regulation for Wind Farms via Stochastic Distribution Control and Image-Based Visual Servoing
abstract: Large-scale wind farms (WFs) are increasingly required to participate in short-term frequency regulation (STFR) during frequency events. To enhance the stability, accuracy, responsiveness, and rapidity of the STFR capability while mitigating the fatigue load of wind turbines, a novel model-free STFR strategy is proposed in this paper based on stochastic distribution control (SDC) theory and image-based visual servoing (IBVS) method for WFs with numerous WTs. The histogram of the frequency is used to guide the WF to implement STFR. By comparing current histogram features with target features, the target frequency histogram tracking control is realized. Meanwhile, by minimizing the active power reference fluctuations for each WT, the fatigue load of each WT is reduced. The optimal active power reference is allocated to individual WTs directly without adopting aggregation and dis-aggregation methods. The simulation results show that the proposed control method improves the STFR capability in terms of stability, accuracy, responsiveness, and rapidity.

title: Task-Difficulty-Guided Multi-Gate Mixture-of-Experts for Robust Uncertainty Quantification in Solar Power Forecasting
abstract: Reliable solar power interval forecasting, critical for grid integration and operational planning, is challenged by quantile heterogeneity and non-Gaussian error distributions. This paper introduces a task-difficulty-guided multi-gate mixture-of-experts (TD-M2oE) framework within paired-quantile multi-task learning. TD-M2oE is characterized by a novel masking gate that adaptively allocates experts across varied quantile tasks, yielding coherent prediction intervals across multiple coverage levels. A composite loss enforces quantile monotonicity and promotes expert diversity, empirically enhancing robustness under non-Gaussian and heteroscedastic conditions. Experiments on real-world solar power datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in interval reliability and sharpness over state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Flexibilizing Grid-Connected Renewable Power to Ammonia Systems via a Novel Hydrogen Storage Design: Configuration and Operational Strategy
abstract: Renewable power to ammonia (ReP2A) offers a promising route for renewable energy utilization. To fully utilize volatile renewable generation without breaking process continuity, ReP2A systems require hydrogen storage subsystems with storage tanks and compressors. However, the conventional layout of hydrogen storage subsystems can cause significant hydrogen supply pressure variations, restricting the ReP2A system to a semi-steady-state operation inadequate for handling renewable fluctuations. In practice, feedforward control based on short-term forecasts is widely employed, yet forecast errors necessitate substantial grid electricity purchases to maintain continuity. This coupling between power and chemical manufacturing increases grid peak-shaving pressure and undermines economic benefits. To address these challenges, a novel hydrogen storage subsystem with a parallel-connected compressor is proposed to enhance pressure regulation, alongside a capacity allocation method and a state-transition-based PID (ST-PID) control strategy. Furthermore, a multi-timescale framework embeds the ST-PID controller to bridge real-time control and long-term optimization. Case studies with real-world data demonstrate that the proposed system unlocks the flexibility for renewable consumption and shows robustness against prediction errors, reducing grid electricity reliance by 38.56% and lowering the levelized cost of ammonia by 8.75%. This offers dual benefits in promoting renewable integration and enhancing economic performance.

title: Power Coupling Mechanism Analysis and Hierarchical Adaptive Decoupling Control for Wind Farm Connected to Weak Grid
abstract: Active frequency and voltage support from wind turbine generators (WTGs) improves grid stability. However, when connected to weak grid, phase-locked loop (PLL) tracking inaccuracies can cause inadequate power decoupling in WTGs. This issue is further aggravated by uneven wind speeds and spatial structure within wind farm (WF), ultimately undermining overall support capability. To address this problem, this paper firstly systematically investigates the influence of multiple factors on the coupling power from the unit, farm, to grid levels. Specifically, PLL bandwidth and grid strength affect the tracking performance of the PLL, while wind speed distribution and spatial structure influence the operating points of WTGs and the coupling transmission between nodes, respectively. On the basis, the Hierarchical Adaptive Decoupling Control (HADC) strategy for WF is proposed, which mitigate the coupling power by introducing quantified power coupling components into the power outer-loop control of rotor-side converter. To improve the applicability and robustness, the main parameters of HADC adaptively vary according to load changes and wind speed distribution. It enables to reduce the power coupling degree and improve frequency and voltage support capability of WF. Finally, case studies are conducted on a real WF project in Bazhou, Xinjiang, China. Simulation results verify the effectiveness of the proposed control method.

title: Event-Driven Restoration of Interconnected Distribution Systems With R-SOPs Adapting to Continuous Disasters and Uncertainties
abstract: Extreme disasters lead to continuous and large-scale faults in distribution systems (DSs), posing challenges in developing practical restoration strategies. This paper proposes a pre-disaster prevention and post-disaster restoration framework for R-SOP-enabled interconnected distribution systems (IDSs), which accounts for the persistence of faults during evolution and the uncertainties in renewable energy source and load. Unlike most existing studies that focus on individual DSs and fixed fault scenarios, this paper employs a reconfigurable soft open point (R-SOP) with asymmetric converter design. Through its feeder selection and converter reconfiguration mechanisms, the R-SOP enables efficient capacity utilization and dynamic interconnection among multiple DSs, and additionally addresses, in a unified manner, the dual uncertainties of stochastic fluctuations and sudden faults under continuous disasters. In the pre-disaster phase, electric buses (EBs) are deployed based on proactive restoration simulations to reduce potential load shedding and shorten post-disaster travel distances. In the post-disaster phase, an event-driven restoration method is developed, wherein predefined fault events and error events dynamically update restoration strategies to adapt to continuous faults and uncertainties. By combining R-SOP-assisted reconfiguration with coordinated scheduling of flexible resources, the proposed method overcomes the limitations of individual-network restoration, enhancing system resilience. Simulation results based on a modified 102-node IDS show that the proposed method not only accelerates service restoration under continuous extreme disaster events but also ensures voltage security.

title: Pre-Trained Invertible Neural Network Assisted High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization Framework for Wind Farm Layout Design
abstract: Wake effects in wind farms degrade energy capture and turbine reliability, underscoring the importance of layout optimization. Existing studies either rely on analytical wake models at the expense of accuracy or combine numerical wake models with heuristic algorithms at the expense of efficiency. In contrast, we propose a pre-trained invertible neural network-assisted high-dimensional Bayesian optimization framework for wind farm layout design, achieving both high accuracy and high efficiency. Specifically, this study employs a high-fidelity numerical wake model to ensure accurate wake estimation and develops a Bayesian optimization (BO)–based framework to enhance search efficiency. An invertible neural network (INN) is specifically designed and, for the first time, integrated with BO to alleviate the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional layout spaces. The proposed INN-BO framework is evaluated under five distinct and progressively complex scenarios, including the real offshore data from California. Comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art algorithms demonstrate that INN-BO achieves superior solution quality with reduced convergence time, highlighting its strong generalizability and practical relevance to real-world wind farm design.

title: A Uniform Grid-Forming Control of Multi-Terminal DC Systems
abstract: The control of a multi-terminal dc (MTDC) system is challenging due to the flexible control modes of AC-DC converter stations at different terminals. In this paper, a uniform grid-forming control method is proposed, which can be applied to all AC-DC converter stations at all terminals of a MTDC system. It can provide the grid-forming and damping effects, and meanwhile achieve the transfer of these effects among the whole system. The different extension formats of the proposed control method are analyzed. The steady-state power flow and the small-signal stability of the whole MTDC system are comprehensively discussed. The time-domain simulations of a five-terminal dc system with renewable energy generation and energy storage are conducted, to validate the corresponding theoretical analysis.

title: BF-YOLO:GIS Inner Surface Detection Model Based on an Improved YOLOv8
abstract: Gas insulated switchgear (GIS) equipment, a crucial component of power grids, requires regular maintenance to ensure stable operation. However, traditional inspection methods have limitations in detecting internal surface defects in GIS pipes, potentially resulting in inefficiencies and safety risks. This paper proposes BF-YOLO, an improved method for internal surface defect detection based on YOLOv8, to address this challenge. BF-YOLO utilizes ShapeIoU loss to focus on edge shapes and scale, enabling more accurate bounding box regression and enhancing detection precision. The FasterNetBlock module helps reduce the model size for more efficient deployment on embedded devices or mobile platforms. The C2F_Faster module further optimizes parameters and model volume while maintaining detection accuracy. Additionally, the reconstructed neck structure, inspired by BiFPN, expands the model's receptive field and enhances spatial information processing, thereby improving the detection of small targets. Compared to the original YOLO model, BF-YOLO demonstrates significant improvements, with mAP@0.5 increasing by 1.1% while the number of parameters and GFLOPs are reduced by 44.1% and 22.2% respectively. These improvements enable faster and more accurate defect detection in GIS pipelines. BF-YOLO provides a valuable solution for automated defect detection, thereby enabling proactive maintenance and enhancing safety and reliability in power grid operations.

title: Single-Terminal Fault Location for Multiterminal HVDCs With Branched Topology
abstract: Research on single-terminal fault locations for multiterminal high-voltage direct current (HVDC) with branched topologies remains limited because i) wave propagation is complicated by impedance discontinuities and line-terminal configurations, hindering universal pattern extraction; and ii) conventional Bergeron method introduces substantial errors for long-distance HVDCs, rendering it unsuitable for single-terminal fault location. To address this, an enhanced Bergeron model (EBM) is first proposed. Frequency-specific propagation delays and losses are incorporated through the Laplace transform and computational circuit inversion. Then, the time-reassigned multi-synchrosqueezing transform (TMSST) processes the guessed wave-process (GWP) and actual wave-process (AWP), reconstructing multi-frequency current waves to label wavefront groups. Reconstructed traveling waves are integrated via weighted least squares (WLS) for robustness. Finally, single-terminal fault location is achieved by optimizing fault distance and fault resistance variables to minimize errors between GWP and AWP. Accurate single-terminal fault location is confirmed in Kunliulong three-terminal HVDC. Without using potential transformers, the method requires only a 2-ms time window and operates reliably under strong noise interferences (with a signal-to-noise ratio as low as 25 dB). Without random forest (RF) correction, non-dead-zone faults show 0.74%-2.81% errors, while dead-zone faults maintain practical applicability with ≤4.22% error. After RF incorporation, the error stays below 0.2% regardless of fault locations.

title: Novel Bushing With Adaptively Field Grading Structure: Simulation and Mechanism
abstract: Bushing has become a critical component endangering the safe functioning of power transmission and limiting its development to higher voltage and power levels. The main technical bottleneck that restricts high voltage bushing is the uneven distribution of electric fields due to its “plug-in” structure. In this paper, a novel adaptive field grading (AFG) bushing with a simple multi-layered structure based on nonlinear materials is introduced. A frequency-domain steady-state simulation method considering the field-dependent dielectric and loss characteristics of nonlinear materials to design the AFG bushing is proposed. Referring to the size of the AC transformer capacitive bushing, the finite element models of the 40.5 kV AFG bushing are established, and the electric field distributions are obtained. Optical electric field sensors are used to test the surface electric field distribution of the bushing samples, validating the accuracy of the simulation method. Combining simulation and experimental test results, the influence of doping concentrations and lengths of the field grading layer on the electric field distribution is studied, and the grading mechanism of nonlinear material is summarized. The results demonstrate the potential of nonlinear materials to relieve electric field concentration in bushings and provide a solid basis for its design and application.

title: An Efficient Unified-Structure Modeling Method for Hybrid MMCs Based on Subdivision States
abstract: Hybrid modular multilevel converters (MMCs), which integrate multiple types of submodules (SMs), exhibit complex switching behaviors and diverse operational states. These characteristics substantially increase the computational burden in electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulation and pose significant challenges for real-time implementation. While existing Thevenin-equivalent models strike a reasonable balance between accuracy and efficiency, their coarse representation of SM states limits further gains in computational performance and hinders extension to new SM topologies, as each requires a topology-specific companion circuit. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an efficient, unified-structure EMT modeling method for hybrid MMCs based on refined SM state decomposition. The proposed approach simplifies the internal equivalent circuits while preserving detailed switching characteristics, enabling a unified mathematical formulation applicable to arbitrary SM types without reconstructing companion circuits. Comparative studies against detailed models in PSCAD demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an accuracy higher than 99.9% while significantly reducing computation time. Furthermore, real-time hybrid digital-physical simulation experiments are conducted on a multi-core CPU platform, benchmarked against the Chongqing-Hubei MMC-HVDC project. Both steady-state power transmission tests and transient power-step experiments confirm that the proposed model completes simulations within a 50 μs time step without overruns, while maintaining deviations within approximately 5% compared to field-recorded waveforms.

title: Field-Validated Accelerometer-Based Tension Estimation for Overhead Distribution Lines
abstract: This paper presents a proof-of-concept framework validated using field data that estimates the mechanical tension and corresponding sag of overhead distribution conductors using on-conductor accelerometers and a Random Forest (RF) model. One minute-resolution datasets were collected over a one-month period from three 30-m spans of a 22.9-kV-class distribution line test facility at the KEPCO Gochang Test Center under non-energized conditions. The direct sensor output channels (AccX, AccY, AccZ, Roll, and Yaw), together with temperature and wind variables, are used as inputs to the RF regressor. Across the three spans under the tested conditions, the RF model achieves the lowest normalized root mean square error and the highest coefficient of determination, with NRMSE in the range of 0.007–0.012 and R2 values approaching unity for tension estimation. Sag is then computed from the estimated tension using a standard parabolic approximation consistent with IEEE Std 524. The resulting sag traces closely match those obtained from measured tension, with R2 between 0.996 and 0.999 and mean sag errors in the few-millimeter range, well within the installation tolerances prescribed by IEEE Std 524. A rolling 5-fold cross-validation analysis shows small fold-to-fold dispersion within the available dataset, supporting the feasibility of the proposed framework as a proof-of-concept under the tested conditions. The proposed framework therefore demonstrates the feasibility of using accelerometer signals for tension and sag estimation and suggests potential applicability to clearance assessment and condition monitoring under similar operating conditions.

title: Observation and Numerical Calculation of Induced Voltage Caused by M Component on 10 kV Overhead Distribution Line
abstract: This article analyzes the lightning-induced voltage (LIV) waveforms generated by M-components recorded by rocket-triggered lightning experiments and performs numerical calculations to investigate the impact of variations in M-component process parameters on the LIV waveforms. The LIVs were measured on a vertically arranged, 1513-meter-long, 10 kV three-phase overhead distribution line. Based on the occurrence time of the M-component, the characteristics of the current waveform, and the polarity of the induced voltage, the M-components measured can be classified into three Types. In addition, this study employs the method of controlling variables and utilizes the hybrid MTL-PEEC (Multi-Conductor Transmission Line – Partial Element Equivalent Circuit) model to analyze the influence of M-component parameters on the induced voltage. The results indicate that an increase in the current rise time leads to a decrease in the absolute value of the negative peak of the induced voltage at the nearest pole, while the positive peak and polarity reversal time increase. An increase in the current half-width results in a longer polarity reversal time and extended decay time after the positive peak. A higher ground reflection coefficient causes increases in both the negative and positive peaks of the induced voltage. Furthermore, an increase in channel height leads to a greater absolute value of the negative peak, a decrease in the positive peak, and a delay in the time to reach peak voltage.

title: Investigation of Metal Particles Behavior in the Interruption of Vacuum Switches
abstract: Late breakdown (LB) following interruption has become a critical limitation to the interruption performance of high-voltage (HV) vacuum interrupters (VIs), with metal particles widely considered as a primary key factor. To investigate the particle behavior in-depth during the interruption process, an optical diagnostic platform was developed to observe the metal particles throughout the entire interruption including arcing and post-arc stages. The particle formation under various electrode erosion modes were comprehensively investigated, and their post-arc motion was analyzed through trajectory tracking. Results show that for axial magnetic field (AMF) electrodes, moderately large currents below the rated short-circuit level can trigger intense cathodic activity, leading to abundant metal particles emission from the molten cathode surface, while the anode remains passive. After the current zero (CZ), once emitted particles collide with the contact surface, the cathode spot particles tend to rebound within the gap or off the chamber wall, while molten pool particles are often reabsorbed by the molten electrode surface. Both types of particles can persist in the gap long after CZ. The combined influence of these cathode particles may act as a primary trigger for LB. This study establishes the correlation between interrupting current, cathode activity, and metal particle generation, along with a detailed characterization of their spatiotemporal behavior during the entire interruption.

title: Discharge-Induced Surface Electrode Degradation in Metallized Film Capacitors: A Comparison Under AC and DC Conditions for UHVDC Applications
abstract: Metallized film capacitors (MFCs) are widely used for DC voltage stabilization and AC harmonic filtering in converter stations of UHVDC systems. However, the growing demand for higher voltage and miniaturization poses challenges to the operating reliability of MFCs. This study employs adaptive signal decomposition denoising and image processing techniques to compare discharge signals and surface electrode degradation of metallized films under DC and AC conditions. A capacitance-reducing discharge (CRD) concept applicable to various operating conditions in converter stations is proposed, encompassing self-healing (SH), flashover around SH points, and margin flashover. Under DC conditions, CRD features high-intensity and more pronounced oscillations. Larger SH points account for 71.2% of capacitance reduction with distinct penetrating flashover paths being observed. Under AC conditions, SH points are smaller and more circular. Frequent flashover discharges cause extensive surface electrode evaporation, with flashover around SH points contributing 40.1% of the overall degradation. The energy of CRD exhibits a power-law relation with the applied voltage, with its exponent factor under DC stress twice that under AC stress. The findings provide theoretical support for the reliability of high-performance MFCs in UHVDC applications.

title: Coordinated Control and Protection Strategy for Transmission Lines Connected to Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: Compared to traditional grid-following (GFL) control, grid-forming (GFM) inverters possess the capability to actively support the grid; however, they retain the inherent characteristics of limited fault current amplitude and controlled phase. To address the degraded adaptability of distance protection on outgoing transmission lines integrated with GFM inverters, this paper proposes a coordinated strategy between GFM control and distance protection. First, based on the compound sequence network, the analytical relationship between the additional reactance component and the fault current phase is analyzed. Consequently, ideal fault current phases required to eliminate measurement errors are derived. Second, an adaptive virtual impedance control-protection coordination strategy based on sequence component separation is proposed. The positive-sequence control loop regulates parameters to track the ideal phase and eliminate the measured reactance error, while the negative-sequence loop suppresses voltage unbalance and provides voltage support. PSCAD/EMTDC simulations demonstrate that, without modifying existing protection configurations or requiring remote communication, the proposed strategy effectively eliminates the impact of the additional reactance. Consequently, it ensures the reliable operation of distance protection and maintains excellent adaptability and reliability in multi-IBR scenarios.

title: Protection of Series-Compensated Transmission Lines Connected to Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: The protection challenges and solutions for series-compensated transmission lines have been thoroughly investigated in the literature. In addition, many studies have highlighted the challenges posed by inverter-based resources (IBRs) to transmission line protection. However, the combined impacts of series compensation and IBRs on transmission line relays remain unexplored. This gap in research has significant practical implications, especially as inverter-based renewable energy sources are often located far from load centers, increasing the probability of series compensation in their vicinity. This paper investigates whether and how existing protection practices for series-compensated lines are influenced by the fault response of IBRs. The findings are relevant not only to the direct tie lines of IBRs but also to lines connected to parts of the grid where the generation is primarily inverter-based. The paper examines the distance and directional elements commonly used for transmission line protection. The analytical studies in this paper are supported by detailed PSCAD/EMTDC simulations of IBRs and series-compensated lines. The paper also presents comprehensive test results from commercial transmission line relays. The results demonstrate that the fault current characteristics of IBRs can invalidate key assumptions underlying existing protection solutions for series-compensated transmission lines, leading to potential misoperations of distance and directional elements. The paper identifies the root causes of these issues and discusses relay configuration strategies to achieve more reliable protection.

title: Redundant Submodule-Based Valve-Side Single-Phase-to-Ground Fault Protection in MMC-MVDC Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a redundant submodule (SM)-based protection scheme for modular multilevel converter-based medium voltage dc (MMC-MVDC) distribution systems under valve-side single-phase-to-ground (SPG) faults. Both symmetrical monopolar and bipolar MMC station configurations are studied, considering half-bridge SMs (HBSMs), full-bridge SMs (FBSMs), and hybrid SMs for each converter station. Redundant SMs normally operate in bypass state and transition into a blocking state once a valve-side SPG fault is detected. In symmetrical monopolar MMCs, the use of unipolar redundant SMs can prevent upper and lower arm overvoltage following converter blocking. However, bipolar redundant SMs are required in the bipolar MMC to mitigate upper arm overvoltage in systems with HBSMs, FBSMs and hybrid SMs, lower arm overvoltage in systems with hybrid SMs, as well as to address the issue of non-zero crossings of grid-side currents in systems with HBSMs. Simulation results in PSCAD/EMTDC validate the effectiveness of the proposed redundant SM-based protection methods for MMC-MVDC distribution systems under valve-side SPG faults.

title: A Fault Location Method Based on Electrode-Seawater Loop Characteristic Frequency Band Signal Injection for Undersea Observation Network
abstract: Submarine cable fault location in undersea observation networks presents significant challenges due to limited measurement data and the complex impedance of the seawater loop. The presence of the frequency-dependent effect of seawater-electrode impedance significantly impacts the accuracy of fault distance measurement, similar to the effect of an unknown transition resistance. This paper proposes a new frequency band signal active injection fault location method. The frequency-dependent characteristics of the submarine cable-electrode-seawater system were analyzed. The electrochemical processes at the electrode-seawater interface, including Faradaic reactions and double-layer effects, were thoroughly investigated. An electrode-seawater impedance model was developed, incorporating seawater impedance, Faradaic impedance, and double-layer capacitance. Based on this model, a full-loop impedance calculation method suitable for DC power supply systems was proposed. The quantitative relationship between fault distance, transition resistance, and the total transmission circuit impedance was further explored. A fault location function was introduced to quantify the correlation between these variables. Using signal injection technology at the shore station, the method effectively overcomes the challenges of data acquisition under limited measurement points and enables accurate location of submarine cable faults. By considering the impedance characteristics of the electrode across different frequency bands and integrating the characteristic impedance and reflection coefficients of the submarine cable, the signal injection frequency range was optimized, significantly improving fault location accuracy. The location function, which is inherently implicit, is solved using the damped nonlinear least-squares iteration method, ensuring efficient and precise fault distance calculation. Study cases demonstrate that this method achieves high-precision fault location in submarine cables and exhibits robustness for various fault locations and resistances.

title: A Novel Protection Method for Hybrid Cascaded UHVDC Line Based on Control Response Characteristics
abstract: To address the issue of long-time protection gap between the traveling wave protection and pilot differential protection actions for high voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines, a novel protection method for hybrid cascaded ultra high voltage direct current (HCUHVDC) line based on control response characteristics is proposed. The variations in the rectifier converter valve trigger angle and the inverter DC current command value are analyzed for faults at different locations. The command value change of DC current is characterized by the time difference between the start of the trigger angle increase and the start of the command value decrease. Characteristic curves of the increment of the trigger angle and the time difference are constructed for forward out-of-zone faults with different fault severity levels on the DC line. The point composed of the trigger angle increment and the time difference for the DC line fault is in the upper right corner of the point for the forward external fault. Based on this feature, a fault identification criterion is constructed. Finally, a ${\pm }$800 kV hybrid cascaded model is built in PSCAD to verify the protection performance. Results show that the proposed scheme can accurately identify DC transmission line faults, with strong robustness against transition resistance and noise interference, thus possessing promising engineering application prospects.

title: Suppression of M 3 C Circulation and Low-Frequency Transmission System Oscillation Based on Dual-Synchronous Coordinate System Circulation Control
abstract: Low-frequency transmission based on a modular multilevel matrix converter (M3C) has gradually become one of the new energy delivery methods because it can reduce transmission frequency and increase transmission capacity. However, there are circulating currents with complex frequency and phase sequence characteristics in the M3C bridge arm, which can seriously affect the performance of the equipment and even cause system oscillation. To address this issue, this paper first establishes a mathematical model of multi-frequency circulation distribution in the M3C and proposes a double synchronous coordinate system circulating current(DSRF-CC) suppression strategy. Secondly, the control loop is mapped to the equivalent circuit of the port and the mechanism of the negative damping that induces system oscillation is revealed. Finally, considering the dual constraints of circulating current (CC) and oscillation suppression, the design region of the circulating current suppression control parameters is quantitatively characterized. The accuracy of the research is verified using MATLAB/Simulink simulations.

title: Mathematical Framework for Harmonic Analysis of Cluster Stream Buffer Switching in MMC HVDC: Chebyshev-Based Approach and Insulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel analytical framework for harmonic characterization of the Cluster Stream Buffer (CSB) switching method in Modular Multilevel Converter (MMC)-based Voltage Source Converters (VSCs). Due to the nonlinear nature of Nearest Level Control (NLC), conventional Fourier-based approaches are not well suited for harmonic analysis of CSB. To address this limitation, a Chebyshev polynomial-based method is proposed, enabling a closed-form representation of harmonic components as functions of the modulation index and switching level. The proposed approach provides improved analytical insight and computational efficiency compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, a design methodology integrating harmonic analysis with dielectric stress evaluation is introduced for optimal switching level selection. The results show that a minimum of 33 levels is required under typical conditions, while higher levels (e.g., 49 levels) may be necessary under increased harmonic stress.

title: Impact of Thermal Cycling Variation on the Static Clamping Pressure in Transformer Test Rig
abstract: During the manufacturing of core-type power transformers, the winding structure is clamped by horizontal clamping beams to withstand operational and through-fault current forces. The effects of evolving grid conditions, e.g., frequent switching cycles and increasingly dynamic load profiles, on the evolution of winding clamping pressure of transformers in operation are largely unknown. This paper investigates how different thermal cycles affect clamping pressure in a pressboard spacer–brass plate stack clamped within a test rig. To minimize the surface effects caused by the sieve structure of the pressboard spacers, the top and bottom cellulose plies have been machined off. In this paper, both oil-impregnated and non-impregnated dry pressboard spacers are studied. All spacers are first vacuum-dried under a constant sizing pressure of 7 MPa, followed by oil-impregnation when applicable. Afterwards, the spacer-brass plate stack is assembled in the test rig with an initial clamping pressure of 4 MPa. To investigate the effect of different thermal cycling on the clamping pressure, three different heating rates are applied: low, medium, and high power. At least 15 heating cycles with a cooling phase in between are applied to each test case. It is observed that the loss of clamping pressure is most pronounced during the first heating cycle and gradually diminishes with subsequent cycles. When the initial effect is excluded, no clear relation between the heating rates and the loss of clamping pressure is observed. No significant influence of oil-impregnation on the evolution of clamping pressure is observed under the present test condition. The results highlight the importance of material treatment and initial clamping procedure during the transformer manufacturing process, as these factors significantly influence the clamping pressure and its long-term stability.

title: Regular Layout Optimization for Offshore Wind Farms Considering Seabed Terrains and Turbulence Intensity
abstract: The offshore wind farm layout optimization (OWFLO) is critical to effectively reducing energy costs. This study presents a planning method for the regular layout of OWF, considering both seabed terrains and turbulence intensity (TI), which is based on a mixed-integer linear fractional programming (MILFP) model. The proposed model considers the life-cycle costs of OWFs, including support structure costs, installation costs, and operation and maintenance (O&M) costs, in which the objective function aims to minimize the levelized cost of energy (LCOE). To address the computational challenges of large-scale OWFLO, we utilize the regular layouts’ “patterns” to reduce the dimensions of decision variables and simplify the power calculation constraints, so that the model can be decomposed and solved by the Bounded Dinkelbach Algorithm (BDA). Finally, the applicability of the proposed model on different terrains is validated through a real OWF in China.

title: Dynamic Thermal Line Rating Estimation of Power System
abstract: Dynamic thermal line rating (DTLR) enhances the power transfer capability of thermally limited overhead lines by accounting for real-time environmental and operational conditions. Key influencing factors include solar irradiance, ambient temperature, line current, wind velocity (wind speed with angular direction), and conductor temperature. While some parameters are readily available via online sources or existing sensors, accurate DTLR estimation typically requires wind and conductor temperature data, which often demand additional instrumentation and cost.
